The good news: it’s the loop you already know. Only the plumbing changes.
So what actually changes?
Random sums become GSM8K: about eight and a half thousand grade-school word problems.
The group size stays at eight. The grader becomes two rewards: format, and correctness.
Answers grow from one token to up to two hundred and fifty-six. And the learning rate becomes tiny: one in a hundred thousand.
Here are the two rewards. Each one gets a batch of answers, and returns one score per answer.
The format reward pays half a point for the exact think-then-answer shape.
The correctness reward pays a full point when the final number matches.
Wait, where does answer come from?
The dataset has a column called answer, and the trainer passes it in by name. The scores add up, so tidy and correct earns one and a half.
And why is format only worth half?
Because if neat paid as much as right, the model could get rich by being neat and wrong.
Now the settings. Two of them set the batch: eight per micro-batch, times two accumulation steps. Sixteen.
So how many questions does each training step see?

Sneaky, isn’t it? It’s B. Batch sizes count answers, not questions.
Sixteen answers is two questions, with a group of eight each. Small, but it’s what fits.
Here’s the rest of the config. You’ve met every knob already.
Num generations is the group size: eight.
Max completion length is the thinking budget: two hundred and fifty-six tokens.
Beta is the leash. We use a small one, zero point zero four, mostly so you can see its curve.
And epsilon is the fence! With the wider top, one point two eight.
Exactly. And the last line is for the T4: f p sixteen on, b f sixteen off.
Even so, training all half a billion numbers means memory for each one, its gradient, and two optimizer notes.
That’s like four copies of the model!
So we freeze the model, and clip a thin, trainable add-on beside some of its layers. It’s called LoRA.
Like clipping a lens onto a camera, instead of rebuilding the camera. About nine million numbers, under two percent of the model.

Free! Switch the add-on off, and there’s the original model.
Last piece: how will you know it worked?
First, a baseline: the untrained model, on two hundred test questions it never trains on.
Then a ten-step smoke test, just to check nothing crashes.
Then the real run: two hundred and fifty steps. Our estimate is roughly an hour. An estimate, not a promise.
And then the same two hundred questions again!
Exactly. The difference is your result. Because the training reward alone can lie.
